source.title: AmpleGCG: Learning a Universal and Transferable Generative Model of Adversarial Suffixes for Jailbreaking Both Open and Closed LLMs

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffixes and an affirmative prefix can elicit harmful responses, using attack success rates rather than the fine-tuning or KL measurements in the original claims.
record.gate_note: The paper does not fine-tune the target chat models or measure aligned-versus-base KL divergence. Its main relevant outcomes are harmful-response ASRs under suffix attacks and an affirmative-prefix condition. It also reports first-token target-rank differences during teacher-forced analysis; that is not a per-token KL result.
record.test_reason: The paper measures how often GCG-style adversarial suffixes, with an optional affirmative phrase appended to the input, get aligned chat models (Llama-2-7B-Chat, Vicuna-7B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4) to produce harmful responses. That bears directly on V4's suffix part. It does no fine-tuning, no aligned-versus-base KL measurement, no parameter localization and no deepening training.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that GCG loss is a poor guide to suffix success, because low-loss suffixes can fail when the first token stays a refusal. Keeping all candidate suffixes raises ASR, and AmpleGCG generates hundreds of suffixes in seconds. These reach near 100% ASR on Llama-2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B and transfer to GPT-3.5 (99% with an affirmative phrase), but not to GPT-4. Query repetition evades a perplexity filter at about 80% ASR.
record.recipe_differences: Uses GCG-optimized adversarial suffixes, suffix generation, and harmful-response ASR evaluation; does not reproduce fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples or measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by target model, attack method, number of sampled suffixes, query set, affirmative prefix, and repetition of the input query. Under perplexity defense, the repetition and suffix-generation variants produce sharply different ASRs.

fits_no_version.finding: For low-loss GCG suffixes that fail on Llama-2-7B-Chat, the teacher-forced rank of the first target token stays high while later target tokens have rank near zero. The model opens with refusal and stays safe. Upweighting the first tokens in GCG did not fix these failures (no numbers given).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal under suffix attack is decided at the first response token; later affirmative tokens are easy once the opening is compliant. This is consistent with shallow alignment but is not a KL comparison with the base model.

record.problems: The authors note that false positives remain in the string- and model-based harmfulness evaluators. Closed-source evaluations use additional evaluators and manual checks, but reported ASRs are not accompanied by uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix D reports additional open-source transfer ASRs; these were left out to retain the main attack, prefix, defense, and first-token-rank results within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning of safety-trained models on harmful examples.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL. Only a teacher-forced target-token rank analysis on failed GCG suffixes (Appendix M).
No prefilling of the assistant's response and no decoding-parameter changes on the victim model. The affirmative phrase is appended to the user input.
No test of whether the data or objective causes shallowness. Remarks on Llama-2 vs Vicuna training differences are speculation.

missing.what: Multi-model AmpleGCG trained on Llama-2-7B-Chat plus Vicuna-7B: Llama-2-7B-Chat ASR rises from 12% (GCG default) to 92% (overgenerate) and 99% (AmpleGCG). Vicuna-7B and Mistral-7B-Instruct are also high.

Transfer ASRs to Mistral-7B-Instruct and cross Llama/Vicuna (e.g. Vicuna-sourced suffixes 0–3% on Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-sourced AmpleGCG 57% on Vicuna-7B). Declared left out in rows_left_out, but the near-zero Vicuna→Llama transfer is a scope limit.
Ablation upweighting the first target tokens in GCG optimization failed to remove first-token refusal; stated only qualitatively.

record.verdict_notes: This is an attack paper that is not one of the original sources. Its affirmative phrase is appended to the user input, so it is not an assistant-prefill test. The perplexity-filter 0% rows measure an external defense, so they are unlinked. The ASR judge combines a keyword list with Beaver-Cost; GPT-4 and human checks are added only for GPT models. The authors acknowledge false positives, and no uncertainty is reported. r39 is recoded from reversed to absent because the difference is 2 of 50 queries.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning of safety-trained target models on harmful examples or measurement of refusal after such fine-tuning.
No fine-tuning of target models on ordinary or carefully selected benign data.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement. The paper's first-token target-rank analysis is a different measure.
Tests adversarial suffix attacks and appending an affirmative prefix to suffixes; does not test victim-side decoding changes or prefill a compliant opening independently of a suffix attack.
No parameter or rank localization or ablation of safety behavior.
Does not test whether safety-training data or objective causes shallow safety behavior. The GCG loss/rank analysis does not establish that causal claim.
No training designed to deepen safety across response positions or test of whether such training holds up.
